author: A Robot
objectives: Determine steric number from a Lewis structure by counting bonding domains and lone pairs around a central atom.
Predict electron-domain geometry from steric number using VSEPR theory for 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 domains.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and predict resulting bond-angle compression.
Apply VSEPR predictions to real molecules and compare predicted shapes with known observed geometries.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: VSEPR Setup and Lewis Structure Input
modules.description: Introduces VSEPR theory and shows how a flat Lewis structure is used to predict 3D molecular shape.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the core VSEPR principle that electron domains minimize mutual repulsion.
Count electron domains from a Lewis structure, treating single, double, triple bonds and lone pairs each as one domain.
Explain that VSEPR predicts three-dimensional geometry from a two-dimensional Lewis structure.
instructions: Look at the central atom and side reference panel.
Use the narration to connect the flat Lewis structure to the 3D prediction process.
Notice that each bond or lone pair counts as one electron domain.

components.text: Central atom
Each bond or lone pair = 1 domain
Oxygen center

clips.changeMeaning: The central atom label is refined to identify the oxygen atom so the learner has an anchor for the upcoming VSEPR explanation.
clips.narration: VSEPR stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion. Its central idea is simple: electron domains around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible.

clips.changeMeaning: The Lewis structure reference panel and counting rule text are emphasized to connect the 2D drawing to the 3D prediction workflow.
clips.narration: We begin with a Lewis structure. In VSEPR, each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair counts as one electron domain around the central atom.

clips.changeMeaning: Electron-domain clouds appear around the oxygen to show the four domains counted from the flat water Lewis structure.
clips.narration: For water, oxygen has two bonding domains and two lone-pair domains, giving a steric number of four. The Lewis structure is flat on paper, but those four domains occupy three-dimensional space.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: Minimum Repulsion with 2 to 4 Domains
modules.description: Shows electron domains spreading out into linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements as domains are added.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate electron-domain repulsion to the formation of stable spatial arrangements.
Identify linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-domain geometries from domain counts of 2, 3, and 4.
Associate idealized bond angles with each arrangement: 180 degrees, 120 degrees, and 109.5 degrees.
instructions: Watch each added domain rearrange the others.
Notice how repulsion vectors appear during motion and fade after stabilization.
Compare the final geometry name and bond angle label after each rearrangement.

components.text: Geometry:
2 domains: Linear, 180°

clips.changeMeaning: Two electron domains move from arbitrary positions to opposite sides of the central atom while a repulsion arrow and geometry label highlight the linear minimum-repulsion arrangement.
clips.narration: With two electron domains, the lowest-repulsion arrangement is linear. The domains settle 180 degrees apart.

components.text: 3 domains: Trigonal planar, 120°

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain appears and all three redistribute into a planar 120-degree pattern, showing how the geometry changes when repulsion must be balanced among three domains.
clips.narration: Adding a third domain changes the arrangement. Three domains minimize repulsion in a trigonal planar geometry, 120 degrees apart in one plane.

components.text: 4 domains: Tetrahedral, 109.5°

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain is added and the domains leave the plane to settle into a tetrahedral arrangement, demonstrating that three-dimensional spacing reduces repulsion further than a flat layout.
clips.narration: With four domains, the best spacing is tetrahedral. The ideal angle between domains becomes about 109.5 degrees.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Completing the Electron-Domain Geometry Catalog
modules.description: Extends the domain count to five and six and summarizes all five electron-domain geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries for steric numbers 5 and 6.
Describe the distinct axial and equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Summarize all five fundamental electron-domain geometries and their characteristic angles.
instructions: Watch how a fifth and sixth domain alter the arrangement.
Rotate your view mentally as narration distinguishes equatorial and axial positions.
Use the summary panel to connect domain count, geometry name, and ideal angles.

components.text: 5 domains: Trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°

clips.changeMeaning: A fifth domain appears and the arrangement reorganizes into three equatorial positions and two axial positions, highlighting the special role of trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
clips.narration: Five electron domains adopt a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. Three lie in an equatorial plane 120 degrees apart, while two occupy axial positions 90 degrees to that plane.

components.text: 6 domains: Octahedral, 90°

clips.changeMeaning: A sixth domain is added so the configuration becomes octahedral, placing every nearest neighbor at right angles in a highly symmetric 3D arrangement.
clips.narration: With six domains, the geometry becomes octahedral. Neighboring domains are arranged at 90-degree angles.

clips.changeMeaning: A side summary panel appears to consolidate all five electron-domain geometries, their domain counts, and ideal angles for comparison.
clips.narration: These five patterns—linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral—form the core electron-domain geometries used in introductory VSEPR predictions.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Electron-Domain Geometry vs Molecular Geometry
modules.description: Compares methane, ammonia, and water to show how lone pairs alter molecular geometry while the electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Identify tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, and bent molecular geometries arising from steric number 4.
Explain why lone pairs are counted for electron-domain geometry but not included as atoms in molecular geometry naming.
instructions: Observe which domains are bonding pairs and which are lone pairs.
Track the labels as the electron-domain geometry stays the same while molecular geometry changes.
Compare methane, ammonia, and water as a sequence built from the same tetrahedral domain arrangement.

components.text: CH4: electron-domain geometry = tetrahedral; molecular geometry = tetrahedral

clips.changeMeaning: The tetrahedral all-bonding case is labeled as methane to establish the baseline where electron-domain and molecular geometry are identical.
clips.narration: In methane, all four tetrahedral domains are bonding pairs. Because every domain leads to a visible atom, the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry are both tetrahedral.

components.text: NH3: electron-domain geometry = tetrahedral; molecular geometry = trigonal pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: One bonded atom is replaced by a lone-pair cloud so the visible atomic arrangement changes to trigonal pyramidal while the underlying tetrahedral domain arrangement is preserved.
clips.narration: Replacing one bonding domain with a lone pair gives ammonia. The electron domains are still tetrahedrally arranged, but the atoms alone trace a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

components.text: H2O: electron-domain geometry = tetrahedral; molecular geometry = bent

clips.changeMeaning: A second bonding domain is replaced by a lone pair, converting the visible atomic arrangement to bent while keeping the same tetrahedral electron-domain framework.
clips.narration: With two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, water still has tetrahedral electron-domain geometry. But because lone pairs are not counted as atoms in the visible shape, the molecular geometry is bent.

modules.description: Compares methane, ammonia, and water side by side to explain why lone pairs compress bond angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Compare ideal and compressed bond angles in methane, ammonia, and water.
Predict the direction of bond-angle change as the number of lone pairs increases.
instructions: Compare the three molecules side by side.
Focus on the sizes of the lone-pair clouds and the angle labels.
Watch the overlay comparison to see bond-angle compression directly.

components.text: More lone pairs → smaller bond angle

clips.changeMeaning: A guiding label is added above the three molecules to direct attention to the trend in bond angles as lone pairs increase.
clips.narration: Compare methane, ammonia, and water. As lone pairs replace bonding pairs, the bond angles decrease from 109.5 degrees to about 107 degrees and then to 104.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The lone-pair-containing molecules are enlarged slightly to emphasize their lone-pair regions and visually support the explanation that lone pairs occupy more angular space.
clips.narration: Lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs because their electron density is held by only one nucleus, so it spreads out more and pushes bonding domains closer together.

clips.changeMeaning: An overlay comparison is introduced so students can directly compare how the observed H-X-H or H-C-H angle narrows as lone pairs are added.
clips.narration: In the overlay view, the trend is easier to see: the visible bond angle compresses as one lone pair and then two lone pairs occupy part of the tetrahedral domain arrangement.

modules.description: Presents example molecules spanning all five electron-domain geometries and several lone-pair-derived molecular geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR reasoning to specific molecules including CO2, BF3, CH4, PF5, SF6, NH3, H2O, and XeF4.
Identify both electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry for each example.
Connect Lewis structures, steric numbers, lone pair counts, and observed 3D shapes.
instructions: Scan the gallery from left to right as the narrator highlights examples.
Compare each 3D model with its Lewis-structure panel.
Notice how different molecules can share an electron-domain geometry but differ in molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.

components.text: CO2 linear | BF3 trigonal planar | CH4 tetrahedral | PF5 trigonal bipyramidal | SF6 octahedral

clips.changeMeaning: The gallery label summarizes one representative all-bonding example for each of the five electron-domain geometries to reinforce the canonical mapping from domain count to arrangement.
clips.narration: Here are representative molecules for the five main electron-domain geometries: carbon dioxide, boron trifluoride, methane, phosphorus pentafluoride, and sulfur hexafluoride.

components.text: NH3 trigonal pyramidal | H2O bent | XeF4 square planar

clips.changeMeaning: The label shifts to highlight lone-pair-derived shapes, and xenon tetrafluoride is moved slightly forward to emphasize square planar geometry as an octahedral-domain derivative.
clips.narration: Lone pairs create additional common shapes. Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, water is bent, and xenon tetrafluoride is square planar even though its electron-domain geometry is octahedral.

components.text: Reasoning: count domains → identify electron-domain geometry → account for lone pairs → name molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: A procedural reasoning label is displayed so students can generalize the same VSEPR workflow across all molecules in the gallery.
clips.narration: For every example, use the same reasoning process: count bonding and lone-pair domains, choose the electron-domain geometry, then remove lone pairs from the visible shape to name the molecular geometry.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7: Prediction Activity - Drag the Domains
modules.description: Students conceptually arrange electron domains into correct VSEPR geometries and then include lone pairs within a tetrahedral arrangement.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recognize target domain arrangements for steric numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.
Use spatial reasoning to place domains in minimum-repulsion positions.
Account for lone pairs when predicting molecular geometry from an electron-domain arrangement.
instructions: Imagine dragging the domains until they are as far apart as possible.
Use the confirmation labels to check whether the arrangement matches the correct geometry.
Pay attention to the final challenge, where one tetrahedral position is a lone pair.

components.text: Arrange 2, 3, and 4 domains as linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral.

clips.changeMeaning: The first activity prompt introduces the basic all-bonding arrangements for two through four domains and reveals the needed movable domains.
clips.narration: First, practice the minimum-repulsion arrangements for two, three, and four domains: linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral.

components.text: Now extend to 5 and 6 domains: trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral.

clips.changeMeaning: Two additional movable domains are enabled so the challenge expands to trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral spatial reasoning.
clips.narration: Next, add a fifth and sixth domain. The correct minimum-repulsion arrangements are trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral.

components.text: Mixed case: 4 domains with 1 lone pair → tetrahedral domains, trigonal pyramidal molecule

clips.changeMeaning: A lone-pair cloud is introduced to shift the challenge from pure electron-domain placement to distinguishing electron-domain geometry from resulting molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Finally, consider a mixed arrangement: four total domains with one lone pair. The electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry becomes trigonal pyramidal.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Prediction Activity - Pick the Correct Structure
modules.description: Students reason from Lewis structures to choose the correct molecular geometry among candidate 3D models.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Determine steric number and lone pair count from unfamiliar Lewis structures.
Select the correct molecular geometry from multiple candidate 3D shapes.
Justify VSEPR predictions for molecules such as SF4, ClF3, BrF5, and I3−.
instructions: Read each Lewis structure, count domains, and identify lone pairs on the central atom.
Compare the candidate models before deciding.
Use the narrated reasoning after each example to verify your logic.

components.text: SF4: 5 domains, 1 lone pair → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry → seesaw molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The first quiz case foregrounds SF4 and subtly advances the seesaw candidate to indicate the correct reasoning path after domain counting and lone-pair analysis.
clips.narration: For sulfur tetrafluoride, count five electron domains around sulfur, with one lone pair. That gives trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry and a seesaw molecular geometry.

components.text: ClF3: 5 domains, 2 lone pairs → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry → T-shaped molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The second quiz swaps in a new Lewis structure and candidate set so students must apply the same VSEPR process to identify a T-shaped molecule derived from trigonal bipyramidal domains.
clips.narration: For chlorine trifluoride, the central chlorine has five domains and two lone pairs. The electron-domain geometry is trigonal bipyramidal, and the molecular geometry is T-shaped.

components.text: BrF5: 6 domains, 1 lone pair → octahedral electron geometry → square pyramidal molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: A final multiple-choice case extends the method to an octahedral-domain example so students see how lone pairs also generate square pyramidal and related shapes from six domains.
clips.narration: For bromine pentafluoride, count six domains and one lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is octahedral, and the molecular geometry is square pyramidal. The same count-first approach works for iodide triiodide and xenon tetrafluoride as well.

modules.description: Reviews the five main concept areas from the lab in a closing summary scene.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the minimum-repulsion principle and the five electron-domain geometries.
Review the distinction between electron-domain and molecular geometry.
Reinforce how lone pairs alter angles and shapes in real molecules.
instructions: Listen for the review of each major idea.
Use the summary board to mentally connect each concept to the earlier scenes.
Prepare to apply the same reasoning sequence on paper Lewis structures after the lab.

components.text: 1. Minimum repulsion principle

clips.changeMeaning: The recap begins by highlighting the first big idea so the closing narration can step through the conceptual arc of the lab in order.
clips.narration: To recap, VSEPR begins with the minimum-repulsion principle: electron domains around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible.

components.text: 2. Five electron-domain geometries and ideal angles

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight advances to the geometry catalog to reinforce the canonical shapes and angle sets students should remember.
clips.narration: Next, remember the five electron-domain geometries: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral, along with their characteristic ideal angles.

components.text: 3. Electron-domain geometry vs molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The recap shifts to the distinction between counting all domains and naming the visible atomic shape, consolidating one of the lab's key conceptual pivots.
clips.narration: Then distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry. Lone pairs count when placing domains, but they are not included when naming the visible shape formed by atoms.

components.text: 4. Lone pairs compress bond angles   5. Apply VSEPR to real molecules

clips.changeMeaning: The final recap highlight combines lone-pair angular effects with real-molecule application so students leave with both mechanistic understanding and practical predictive workflow.
clips.narration: Finally, lone pairs occupy more angular space and compress bond angles, and the full VSEPR method can be applied to real molecules by counting domains, identifying the electron-domain geometry, and then naming the molecular geometry.
